{{Short description|Constructions in nonsmooth analysis}}

In [[variational analysis]], [[Set-valued function|set-valued]] analysis and [[Mathematical optimization|optimization]], the concept of a '''normal cone''' to a subset of a space generalizes that of the [[orthogonal complement]] / [[Dual space#Annihilators|annihilator]] of a vector space, [[Normal (geometry)#Normal to general surfaces in 3D space|(outward) normal vector fields]] to surfaces — or more generally of the [[normal bundle]] of an embedded [[submanifold]] — to possibly non-smooth subsets of [[vector space]]s.

Normal cones provide, among other things, the geometrical foundation for generalizing the [[Subderivative|convex subdifferential]] to non-convex functions. Of particular note is also their role in generalizing '''[[Interior extremum theorem|Fermat's rule]]''' to give necessary (and sometimes also sufficient) first order optimality conditions for constrained and non-smooth optimization problems. Moreover, they play a role in defining coderivatives of set-valued maps.<ref name=":1" />

In the non-convex case there are several inequivalent definitions for a normal cone that all turn out to be useful and interesting for different problems — whereas in the convex case these all coincide which greatly simplifies things. For clarity and approachability this article first discusses the convex case over [[Hilbert space]]s before going into the non-convex case over more general spaces.

== Conventions ==
All vector spaces in this article are assumed to be real. The set <math>\bar{\R}</math> denotes the [[Extended real number line|extended real numbers]] and a function <math>f : X \to \bar{\R}</math> is called ''[[Proper convex function|proper]]'' if it is nowhere equal to <math>-\infty</math> and also somewhere finite. We also assume that all cones contain zero. Sums of sets throughout the article are to be interpreted as [[Minkowski addition|Minkowski sums]].

[[File:Normal Cone Example.pdf|thumb|A set <math>C \subseteq \R^2</math> together with the normal cone at one of its points.]]

== Convex Case ==

=== Definition ===
The '''convex normal cone''' <math>N_C^\operatorname{conv}</math> to a non-empty [[Convex set|convex subset]] <math>C \subseteq H</math> of a [[Prehilbert space|(pre-)Hilbert space]] is defined by<math display="block">\begin{alignat}{2}
N_C^\operatorname{conv}(\bar{x}) :=& \{v \in H : \langle v, x - \bar{x} \rangle \leq 0 ~\text{for all}~ x \in C \}
\\ =& \{v \in H : \sup_{x \in C} \langle v, x - \bar{x} \rangle \leq 0\}
\end{alignat}</math>for all <math>\bar{x} \in C</math>, and <math>N_C^\operatorname{conv}(\bar{x}) = \emptyset</math> for all <math>\bar{x} \not\in C</math>.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Rockafellar |first=Ralph Tyrell |title=Convex Analysis |date=2015 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=978-0-691-01586-6 |series=Princeton Landmarks in Mathematics and Physics |location=Princeton}}</ref><ref name=":0" /> Here <math>\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle : H \times H \to \R
</math> denotes the [[Inner product space|inner product]] of <math>H</math>.

==== Geometric Interpretation ====
This definition can intuitively be understood as follows: suppose <math>\bar{x}, x \in C</math> and <math>v \in H</math>, then <math>x-\bar{x}</math> is the vector from <math>\bar{x}</math> to <math>x</math>. If <math>\langle x - \bar{x}, v \rangle = 0</math> then <math>x - \bar{x}</math> would be orthogonal to <math>v</math>, while the condition <math>\langle x - \bar{x}, v \rangle \leq 0</math> additionally allows <math>v</math> to "point away" from <math>x-\bar{x}</math> more than 90°. So the (convex) normal cone at <math>\bar{x}</math> is the set of all vectors <math>v</math> that point at least 90° away from all the vectors from <math>\bar{x}</math> to <math>C</math>; but translated to the origin.

=== Examples ===
* When <math>C</math> is a subspace of <math>H</math>, then <math>N_C^\operatorname{conv}(\bar{x}) = C^\bot</math> is the linear-algebraic normal space / [[orthogonal complement]] to <math>C</math> for <math>\bar{x} \in C</math>. If <math>C</math> is instead an [[Affine space|affine subspace]] then <math>N_C^\operatorname{conv}(\bar{x})</math> is instead the orthogonal complement to the underlying parallel vector space of <math>C</math>.
* Let <math>C \subseteq H</math> be a non-empty, closed, convex set and consider its convex indicator function <math>\delta_C(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & x \in C \\ +\infty & x \in H \setminus C \end{cases}.</math> Then <math>\partial \delta_C = N_C^\operatorname{conv}.</math>
* For a proper, [[Semi-continuity|lower-semicontinuous]], convex function <math>f : H \to \bar{\R}</math> we have <math>s \in \partial f(\bar{x}) \iff (s,-1) \in N_{\operatorname{epi}(f)}^\mathrm{conv}(\bar{x}, f(\bar{x}))</math>, where <math>\operatorname{epi}(f) \subseteq H \times \R</math> denotes the [[Epigraph (mathematics)|epigraph]] of <math>f</math> and <math>\partial f</math> the convex subdifferential of <math>f</math>. This relationship serves to define further subdifferentials based on normal cones in the non-convex case.

=== Properties ===
* <math>N_C^\operatorname{conv}(\bar{x})</math> is a non-empty, convex cone for all <math>\bar{x} \in C</math>.
* If <math>\dim(H) < \infty, \bar{x} \in C</math>, then <math>\bar{x} \in \operatorname{int}(C) \iff N_C^\operatorname{conv}(\bar{x}) = \{0\}</math>.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Bauschke |first=Heinz H. |url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-3-319-48311-5 |title=Convex Analysis and Monotone Operator Theory in Hilbert Spaces |last2=Combettes |first2=Patrick L. |date=2017 |publisher=Springer International Publishing |isbn=978-3-319-48310-8 |series=CMS Books in Mathematics |location=Cham |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-48311-5}}</ref> The forward direction <math>(\Rightarrow)</math> holds even if <math>H</math> is infinite dimensional, while the backward direction <math>(\Leftarrow)</math> may fail unless <math>C</math> has nonempty interior.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Mordukhovich |first=Boris S. |url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-3-030-94785-9 |title=Convex Analysis and Beyond: Volume I: Basic Theory |last2=Mau Nam |first2=Nguyen |date=2022 |publisher=Springer International Publishing |isbn=978-3-030-94784-2 |series=Springer Series in Operations Research and Financial Engineering |location=Cham |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-94785-9}}</ref>
* Let <math>C \subseteq H
</math> be non-empty, closed, convex. Then <math>c = \operatorname{proj}_C(x^*) \iff x^* - c \in N_C^\operatorname{conv}(c)</math>, where <math>\operatorname{proj}_C(x^*)</math> is the [[metric projection]] of <math>x^*</math> onto <math>C</math>.<ref name=":0" />
* '''Intersection Rule''': <math>N_{C_1 \cap C_2}^\operatorname{conv}(\bar{x}) \supseteq N_{C_1}^\operatorname{conv}(\bar{x}) + N_{C_2}^\operatorname{conv}(\bar{x})</math> for any two nonempty, convex subsets <math>C_1, C_2 \subseteq X</math> of a tvs <math>X</math> and <math>\bar{x} \in C_1 \cap C_2</math>. Provided that the qualification condition <math>\operatorname{int}(C_1) \cap C_2 \neq \emptyset </math> holds, the reverse inclusion is also true such that <math display="block">N_{C_1 \cap C_2}^\operatorname{conv}(\bar{x}) = N_{C_1}^\operatorname{conv}(\bar{x}) + N_{C_2}^\operatorname{conv}(\bar{x}).</math>The qualification condition may be further weakened, especially if <math>X</math> is a nicer space.<ref name=":2" /> For example, if <math>X</math> is Banach and the two convex sets are closed, it is sufficient that <math>0 \in \operatorname{int}(C_1 - C_2)</math>, while in finite dimensions one can show that  <math display="block">N_{\bigcap_i C_i}^\operatorname{conv}(\bar{x}) = \sum_i N_{C_i}^\operatorname{conv}(\bar{x})</math>for any finite family of convex sets <math>(C_i)_i</math> whose [[relative interior]]s intersect.
* For further calculus rules cf. the properties of the non-convex generalizations below.
Another very important property is what is sometimes called '''Fermat's rule''': let <math>f : H \to \R</math> be convex, <math>C \subseteq H</math> nonempty, closed and convex. Then, assuming some very mild [[constraint qualification]]s (c.f. for example Proposition 27.8 in <ref name=":0" />), <math>\bar{x} \in H</math> solves the constrained minimization problem <math>\min_{x \in C} f(x)</math> if and only if <math>0 \in \partial f(\bar{x}) + N_C^\operatorname{conv}(\bar{x})</math>. If <math>f</math> is differentiable this reduces to <math>- \nabla f(\bar{x}) \in N_C^\operatorname{conv}(\bar{x})</math> (here <math>\nabla f</math> is the Fréchet gradient of <math>f</math>; i.e. the pointwise [[Riesz representation theorem|Riesz representative]] of the [[Fréchet derivative]] of <math>f</math>).

=== Generalization ===
More generally, one may define <math display="block">N_C^\operatorname{conv}(\bar{x}) := \{\varphi \in X^* : \langle \varphi, x - \bar{x} \rangle \leq 0 ~\text{for all}~ x \in C \} = \{\varphi \in X^* : \sup_{x \in C} \langle \varphi, x - \bar{x} \rangle \leq 0\}</math>for any [[topological vector space]] <math>X</math>, with [[topological dual]] <math>X^*</math>. In this case <math>\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle : X^* \times X \to \R, (\varphi, x) \mapsto \varphi(x)</math>  is the [[duality pairing]] of <math>X</math> and <math>X^*.</math> In this more general setting the normal cone can be recognized to be the set of all <math>\varphi \in X^*</math> that attain their maximum on <math>C</math> at <math>\bar{x}</math>.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Penot |first=Jean-Paul |url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-1-4614-4538-8 |title=Calculus Without Derivatives |date=2013 |publisher=Springer New York |isbn=978-1-4614-4537-1 |series=Graduate Texts in Mathematics |volume=266 |location=New York, NY |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-1-4614-4538-8}}</ref> This connects normal cones to another important class of objects, the so-called [[support function]] <math>\sigma_C</math> of a set. One has <math>\varphi \in N_C^\operatorname{conv}(\bar{x}) \iff \varphi(\bar{x}) = \sigma_C(\varphi)</math>.

== Non-Convex Case ==
In the remainder of this article we will assume the space we're working on to be [[Asplund space|Asplund]] for ease of exposition. While some of the following definitions and properties are fine / remain true for more general spaces (e.g. general normed spaces), this is not true for all of them. The class of Asplund spaces contains many important [[Banach space]]s, for example all [[Lp space|<math>L^p</math>-spaces]] for <math>p \in (1, \infty)</math>, but '''not''' the cases <math>p \in \{1, \infty\}.</math>

=== Definition ===
Let <math>X</math> be an Asplund space with topological dual <math>X^*</math> and <math>A \subseteq X</math> a (potentially non-convex) nonempty subset of <math>X</math>. There are three main normal cones defined for this case:

# The '''Fréchet normal cone''' <math>N_A^F</math> is defined by <math display="block">N_A^F(\bar{x}) := \{ \varphi \in X^* : \limsup_{x \to \bar{x}, x \neq \bar{x}} \frac{\langle \varphi, x - \bar{x} \rangle}{\lVert x - \bar{x} \rVert} \leq 0 \}</math>for any <math>\bar{x} \in \operatorname{cl} A</math>, and empty outside of that. Alternatively it may be defined as the [[Dual cone and polar cone|polar]] of the [[Paratingent cone|'''Bouligand tangent cone''']] <math>T_A(\bar{x}) = \{x \in X : \exists (x^k) \subseteq X, \exists (t_k) \searrow 0 : x^k \to x \text{ and } \bar{x} + t_k x^k \in A \}</math>.<ref name=":1" /> Note that these definitions generally only coincide if <math>A</math> is closed. Alternatively one may define <math display="inline">\begin{alignat}{2}
N_A^F(\bar{x}) &:= \{ \varphi \in X^* : \langle \varphi, x - \bar{x} \rangle \leq o(\lVert x - \bar{x} \rVert) ~\text{as}~ x \to_A \bar{x} \}
\end{alignat}</math>where <math>o(\lVert x - \bar{x} \rVert) ~\text{as}~ x \to_A \bar{x}</math> denotes a "small-o" [[Big O notation#Little-o notation|Landau symbol]]; this in turn is equivalent to the first definition.<ref name=":3" />
# The '''Mordukhovich (or limiting) normal cone''' <math>N_A^M</math> is defined by <math display="block">N_A^M(\bar{x}) := \operatorname{Lim\,sup}_{x \to_A \bar{x}} N_A^F(x) = \{\varphi \in X^* : \exists (x^k) \subseteq X : \exists (\varphi^k) \subseteq X^* : x^k \to_X \bar{x}, \varphi^k \to \varphi, \varphi^k \in N_A^F(x^k) \}.</math> Here <math>\operatorname{Lim\,sup}</math> is an [[Limit inferior and limit superior#General set convergence|outer limit]] of sets where X carries its usual norm topology while <math>X^*</math> is endowed with its [[Weak topology#Weak-* topology|weak* topology]] and the notation <math>x \to_A \bar{x}</math> means that "<math>x</math> converges to <math>\bar{x}</math> along <math>A</math>", i.e. the sequence of points in the definition of the outer limit is a sequence of points in <math>A</math>.
# The '''Clarke normal cone''' <math>N_A^C</math> is defined by <math display="block">N_A^C(\bar{x}) := \operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}(N_A^M(\bar{x}))),</math>where <math>\operatorname{cl}</math> is the [[Closure (topology)|topological closure]] and <math>\operatorname{conv}</math> the [[convex hull]] of a set.
These normal cones form a nested hierarchy <math>N_A^F(\bar{x}) \subseteq N_A^M(\bar{x}) \subseteq N_A^C(\bar{x})</math>.

==== Alternate names and notation ====
The Fréchet normal cone is also called the ''firm'', ''regular'' and ''prenormal'' Normal cone in the literature and oftentimes denoted by <math>\hat{N}_A(\bar{x}).</math> The Mordukhovich normal cone is also called the limiting or ''basic'' normal cone and sometimes denoted by <math>N_A(\bar{x})</math> or <math>N_A^L(\bar{x})</math>. The Clarke normal cone is also called the ''convexified'' normal cone and sometimes denoted by <math>\bar{N}_A(\bar{x}).</math><ref name=":3" /><ref>{{Cite book |last=Mordukhovich |first=Boris S. |url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-3-031-53476-8 |title=Second-Order Variational Analysis in Optimization, Variational Stability, and Control: Theory, Algorithms, Applications |date=2024 |publisher=Springer International Publishing |isbn=978-3-031-53475-1 |series=Springer Series in Operations Research and Financial Engineering |location=Cham |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-031-53476-8}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Clarke |first=Francis |url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-1-4471-4820-3 |title=Functional Analysis, Calculus of Variations and Optimal Control |date=2013 |publisher=Springer London |isbn=978-1-4471-4819-7 |series=Graduate Texts in Mathematics |volume=264 |location=London |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-1-4471-4820-3}}</ref>

== Comparison of Fréchet, Mordukhovich and Clarke normal cones for applications to optimization ==
Suppose, for simplicity, that we have some Fréchet differentiable function <math>f : X \to \R</math> and consider the stationarity condition <math>-\nabla f(\bar{x}) \in N_A(\bar{x})</math> corresponding to each of the three normal cones. If <math>N_A(\bar{x})</math> is "too large" — in the extreme case we may even find that <math>N_A(\bar{x}) = X</math> — we can't expect these conditions to actually tell us anything about the (non-)optimality of <math>\bar{x}</math>. Conversely, if <math>N_A(\bar{x})</math> is "too small" — in the extreme case we might find it to be empty or to only contain zero — we will find it difficult or even impossible to verify that  <math>-\nabla f(\bar{x}) \in N_A(\bar{x})</math>, or to computationally determine <math>\bar{x}</math> such that this holds. Because of this (and differences in their associated calculi) all three cones (as well as further ones) have their place in the theory and applications.

== Examples ==
* Let <math>A = \{(x,y) \in \R^2 : xy = 0, y \geq 0 \}</math>. Then, identifying <math>(\R^2)^* \simeq \R^2</math>, we have <math>N_A^F(0) = \{0\} \times (-\infty, 0]</math>, <math> N_A^M(0) = \{xy = 0\}</math> and <math>N_A^C(0) = \R^2.</math>
* Suppose <math>X \subseteq \R^n</math> is a smooth embedded submanifold. Let <math>p \in X</math> and denote by <math>N_p X \subseteq T_p \R^n</math> the normal space of <math>X</math> at <math>p</math>. Then <math>N_p X \simeq_\mathbf{Vect} N_X^F(p) = N_X^C(p) = N_X^M(p)</math>.<ref name=":3">{{Cite book |last=Rockafellar |first=R. Tyrrell |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-3-642-02431-3 |title=Variational Analysis |last2=Wets |first2=Roger J. B. |date=1998 |publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg |isbn=978-3-540-62772-2 |series=Grundlehren der mathematischen Wissenschaften |volume=317 |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-02431-3}}</ref>

== Properties ==
* The inclusions <math>N_A^F(\bar{x}) \subseteq N_A^M(\bar{x}) \subseteq N_A^C(\bar{x})</math> always hold, in general they are strict.
* <math>N_A^F(\bar{x})</math> may be trivial, while <math>N_A^M(\bar{x})</math> is always nontrivial provided that <math>\dim(X) < \infty</math>, <math>A</math> is closed and <math>\bar{x} \in \operatorname{bd}(A)</math>.
* Since the Clarke normal cone is always convex it can often end up being "too large" in practice and may degenerate to <math>N_A^C(\bar{x}) = X^*</math>. In contrast to this, the Mordukhovich normal cone can be nonconvex which allows it to remain "small enough to be useful" in some cases where Clarke is too large.
* It holds that <math>N_A^C(\bar{x}) = ((N_A^M(\bar{x}))_\circ)^\circ</math> where <math>S_\circ \subseteq X</math> is the prepolar of a set <math>S \subseteq X^*</math> and <math>T^\circ \subseteq X^*</math> is the polar of a set <math>T \subseteq X</math> so that <math>N_A^C(\bar{x})</math> is the [[Bipolar theorem|bipolar]] of <math>N_A^M(\bar{x})</math>.
* Let <math>C \subseteq X</math> be a convex set, then <math>N_C^\operatorname{conv} = N_C^F = N_C^M = N_C^C</math>.
* <math>N_A^M</math> is stable, that is <math>N_A^M(\bar{x}) = \operatorname{Lim\,sup}_{x \to_A \bar{x}} N_A^M(x).</math>
* Let <math>X</math> be Hilbert, <math>C \subseteq X
</math> non-empty and closed, and suppose <math>c \in \operatorname{proj}_C(x^*)</math>. Then <math>x^* - c \in N_C^F(c)</math>. (Note that in contrast to the convex case this fails to be an equivalence in general. Moreover, if <math>X</math> is infinite dimensional there may be no such <math>c</math>)
* '''Product Rule''': <math>N_{A_1 \times A_2}^F(\bar{x}_1, \bar{x}_2) = N_{A_1}^F(\bar{x}_1) \times N_{A_2}^F(\bar{x}_2)</math> for any two nonempty, closed subsets <math>A_1, A_2 \subseteq X</math>, <math>\bar{x}_1 \in A_1, \bar{x}_2 \in A_2</math> of a normed space <math>X</math>. The analogous statement holds for <math>N_{A_1 \times A_2}^M</math>.<ref name=":1" />
* '''Intersection rule''': Suppose <math>(A_i)_i</math> is a finite family of closed subsets in <math>X</math> that is ''allied'' at <math>\bar{x} \in \bigcap_i A_i</math>. Then<math display="block">N_{\bigcap_i C_i}^\operatorname{conv}(\bar{x}) \subseteq \sum_i N_{C_i}^\operatorname{conv}(\bar{x})</math>holds. Alliedness is a somewhat lengthy, technical condition that may be found in Penot's book. Alternatively one may assume the so-called ''Fuzzy qualification condition''.<ref name=":1" />
* '''Chain Rule''': Let <math>F : \R^n \to \R^m</math> be a <math>C^1</math>-function, and <math>C = \{x \in A : F(x) \in D\}</math> where <math>A, D</math> are closed in <math>\R^n, \R^m</math> respectively. Then <math display="block">N_C^M(\bar{x}) = N_A^M(\bar{x}) + F'(\bar{x})^* N_D^M(F(\bar{x})),</math> subject to some constraint qualifications and regularity conditions.<ref name=":3" /> Here <math>F'</math> is the [[Jacobian matrix and determinant|Jacobian]] of <math>F</math>.
